# Cervical myelopathy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Spinal cord disorders > Cervical myelopathy*

[Original Article Link](/library/X509ig)

---

## Summary

Cervical <u>myelopathy</u> is a type of <u>myelopathy</u> that is caused by axonal injury of the cervical spinal cord, either by direct compression or <u>ischemic</u> injury due to compression of the <u>anterior spinal artery</u>. The most common cause is <u>cervical spondylotic myelopathy</u>. Other etiologies include spinal trauma, <u>neoplasms</u>, epidural <u>abscess</u>, and autoimmune disorders. Onset can be acute, insidious, or progress in a stepwise fashion. Clinical features include <u>neck pain</u> and stiffness, impaired sensation in the hands and arms, <u>weakness</u>, poor manual dexterity, and gait instability. The diagnosis is confirmed by <u>MRI</u>. Treatment includes <u>conservative management</u> for mild disease without functional impairment or surgical decompression in acute or severe disease with functional impairment.

---

## Etiology

* Cervical spondylotic myelopathy (most common)

* Compression of the cervical spinal cord as a result of a degenerative process

* Typically occurs in adults > 50 years of age

* Trauma (e.g., <u>fracture</u>, <u>epidural hematoma</u>)

* Tumors (e.g., <u>meningiomas</u>, nerve sheath tumors, <u>metastases</u>, <u>epidermoid cysts</u>)

* <u>Spinal epidural abscess</u>

* <u>Radiation therapy</u>

* Autoimmune disorders (e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>)

* Discogenic <u>myelopathy</u> (central <u>disk herniation</u>)

* Cervical <u>kyphosis</u>

* Congenital <u>spinal stenosis</u>

* <u>Ossification</u> of the <u>posterior longitudinal ligament</u> (OPLL)

## Clinical features

Clinical features depend on the level of compression. Symptoms may be acute in onset (e.g., with trauma) or progress slowly (e.g., degenerative diseases) or in a step-wise fashion.




* <u>Neck pain</u> and stiffness

* Occipital <u>headache</u> (common)

* Axial <u>neck pain</u>

* Impaired sensation in the hands and arms (e.g., diffuse numbness, <u>paresthesias</u>)

* Gait instability (often an early sign), impaired <u>proprioception</u>

* <u>Weakness</u> and clumsiness (poor manual dexterity) in the hands and arms

* Signs and symptoms of <u>lower motor neuron lesions</u> at the level of the lesion (e.g., <u>weakness</u> and <u>atrophy</u> in the arms and/or hands, <u>hyporeflexia</u>)

* Signs and symptoms of an <u>upper motor neuron lesion</u> below the level of the lesion (e.g., <u>weakness</u>, increased tone, <u>hyperreflexia</u>, or a positive <u>Babinski sign</u>)

* Positive <u>Lhermitte sign</u>

* Impaired <u>bladder</u> and bowel control (rare)





> [!TIP]
> Injury to the spinal cord and the <u>nerve roots</u> (<u>radiculopathy</u>) often occurs simultaneously!




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Pain</u> is often absent in early stages. Therefore, a high index of suspicion is needed to make an early diagnosis and prevent progression of functional impairment due to <u>spinal cord injury</u>!
